title: tactical vs emergency vs retention reloads
text: Tactical vs. Emergency vs. Retention Reloads Though they're not specific techniques, tactical and emergency reloads are widely practiced, trained, and discussed by firearms users worldwide. An emergency reload is exactly what it sounds like, but let is flying and the ammunition runs out. Normally, when changing magazines, the empty one is stowed away. They are reusable after all. In an emergency, this is done away with. The mag drops, a new one is slammed in as quickly as possible, and the next round chambered and sent down range in a hurry. It isn't graceful, just sheer practicality in an intense situation. When things are marginally calmer, there is a tactical reload. After firing a few rounds, if there's a lull in the fighting, a new magazine is drawn, the partially empty magazine is ejected, and the fresh one inserted with a round already in the chamber. No cocking needed. This way, should things go south, there's a full magazine in place, ready to go in the middle of a firefight. The tactical reload can be done, while juggling both the new and half-used magazine at the same time. Grab a new magazine with the offhand, place it next to the magazine well, eject the old mag and catch it, then slide in the new one before stowing the partial magazine. This can be a bit awkward and need some practice. The retention reload is similar, but it involves ejecting the old magazine, stowing it away properly, then inserting the full magazine. A bit slower, but much easier. In both the tactical and retention reloads, the ammunition in the half-empty magazines are still available and ready to be used if needed. A full magazine is better than a partially empty one, but a partial magazine is better than not at all. Firearm instructors may use different methods and may mix the terminology a bit, but all are ways to reload in a hurry.

title: WWII “Medic Powder”: Sulfa Powder Explained
text: Sulfa Powder and Shrimp Shells Most people have seen war movies where a medic sprinkles a powder on a wound before treating a casualty. What was that substance and why did they do it? Infection has been the bane of army since the dawn of time, causing more deaths than the wounds themselves. This issue was under control with the introduction of antibiotics. During the Second World War, the US used crystallized sulfanilamide and sulfadiazane tablets, and each soldier would be issued with a single-use dose of each, along with a compression bandage. When wounded, the packet of crystallized sulfanilamide powder would be emptied onto the wound, covered with the bandage, and the soldier would take the tablets. These measures would hopefully kill off any bacteria in the wound and prevent infections and were largely successful in doing so. The sulfadiazane tablets were not to be used on soldiers with abdominal wounds, since nausea and stomach cramps were a common side effect, which would only make the wound worse. Furthermore, the sulfa powder only disinfects the outside of the wound and does little to prevent infection deep inside the wound. It wasn't a bad idea and certainly was better than nothing, but by the end of the war, sulfa powder was slowly phased out in favor of more substantial antibiotics such as penicillin. Today, medics are more concerned with stopping the bleeding and will deal with infections later. To stop hemorrhaging, they use procedures like direct pressure, tourniquets, and chemical assistance. Kiolin is a mineral mostly used in porcelain, but also has uses in paper and rubber manufacturing and the cosmetic industry. Kaitazan is a compound derived from the shells of marine crustaceans like shrimp and crabs. Both have hemostatic properties, which means they help slow down bleeding. Kiolin-treated gauze and kaitazan gels and powders have been and continue to be used both by civilian and military medical practitioners, including combat medics. In combat zones, medics use kale and treated gauze and kaitazan gels and powders, which helps slow down the bleeding much more than pressure and tourniquets alone, causing clotting up to many times faster than direct pressure alone. While infection is a concern, stopping the bleeding is much higher on the list of priorities, and any infection can be treated later with antibiotics.

title: What Are The 6 Levels Of Automated Driving?
text: There are six levels of automated driving, and despite the countless promises you've heard, most vehicles today only reach level 2, as defined by SAE. The foundation for all automated driving comes from Advanced Driver Assistance Systems, or ADAS. ADAS uses sensors, like cameras and radar to gather data, processors to interpret data and plan actions, and control systems to steer, brake, or accelerate. How much of that work the driver still handles determines the automation level. At levels 0 through 2, the driver stays fully responsible, even if the car might be controlling the steering or vehicle speed. As an example, Qualcomm offers their Snapdragon Ride platform, where manufacturers like BMW, with their new Ix3, can choose which ADAS features they want implemented on their vehicle. Level 3 means the car is driving itself, but you need to be ready to take over if it asks for your help. Finally, levels 4 and 5 remove the need for a driver altogether, and possibly even the pedals and steering wheel. At which point, you're just cargo that happens to have opinions, and not even good ones.

title: Why Jet Engines have a Speed Limit
text: Jet engines need to compress air before it enters the combustion chamber in order to extract as much energy as possible from the fuel. A normal jet engine does this with a compressor section where air enters the engine and is squeezed down into a smaller volume by the compressor blades. The compressor is driven by the turbines which extract some of the energy released in the combustion chamber to drive the compression stage. This type of engine has a speed limit because of all of those moving rotating parts. As the speed of the aircraft increases, the incoming air is compressed more and more as it's forced down the inlet of the engine, which results in ever increasing temperatures, which can eventually exceed the material limits of the compressor and turbine blades. Ram jets get around this by using the forward motion of the plane to ram air directly into the combustion chamber. So, we don't need any of the compressors or turbines at all. The forward motion of the plane provides enough compression alone.

title: Is Skipping Gears Bad For Your Manual Transmission?

title: Why Power Shifting Is A Terrible Idea
text: Don't shift like a noob. Power shift. This is actually bad advice unless your car is tuned for it. Power shifting is just like regular shifting in a manual transmission, but you never lift your foot off the gas pedal. The clutch goes in and out, while your right foot remains planted and the gear shift is executed. The problem is if you keep the gas pedal down while shifting, your engine RPM goes up, but your transmission wants a lower RPM. So this discrepancy is handled by the clutch, creating a shock load within the system. But you can design your way out of this. On cars like this Cadillac, which comes with flat foot shifting from the factory, once you press the clutch in, the spark plug firing is delayed. So instead of the engine creating a lot of torque and thus a terrible shock load, that energy instead goes out the exhaust, conveniently keeping the turbochargers spooled up during the shift. title: Could identical twins commit the perfect crime?
text: Could identical twins get away with murder? Identical twins have the same DNA, so if one of them commits a murder, which one goes to prison? Across three billion base pairs, twins may differ in roughly five positions. Now in the unique case of twin suspects, scientists can now use whole genome sequencing, which reads all three billion base pairs to try and find the differences. After a couple of weeks, the renovations on Tamara's home were complete, but Tamara didn't want to leave. A couple of months go by and Tamara is showing no sign that she plans on leaving Valentina's home anytime soon. Finally, in late July 2015, Valentina confronts Tamara and says, you gotta go. And Tamara just says, no, I'm not leaving. This causes a huge fight, but at the end of it, Tamara still doesn't leave. The silence is finally broken on July 23rd when the women get into a fight about some empty cups in the sink that one of them was supposed to clean. But at the end of this fight, Tamara finally concedes and says, okay, I get it, I need to leave, just give me a couple of days and I'll be out of your hair. Immediately, the tension is gone in the room and Tamara says, look, I'll make us dinner tonight, I'll go out and get some food. Tamara leaves the apartment and goes to a pharmacy and gets a whole bunch of sleeping pills. She goes back, she starts making dinner and as she's making the salad, she crushes up the sleeping pills and mixes the powder with the salad dressing and gives that to Valentina. As soon as Tamara was sure Valentina had eaten the entire salad, Tamara just goes up to her room and goes to bed. They're kind of sensitive with her and they say, your friend, your relative was just found deceased and we need to look around the apartment. Tamara was completely indifferent. She did not care. During the search, the police officers quickly find blood all over the bathroom and in the kitchen. They even find the hacksaw she used that's got blood on it and they find Tamara's diary that's sitting next to this book about black magic. And the police are horrified when they see that the diary contains meticulous notes that Tamara had kept of all of the ritualistic killings she had perpetrated over the past 20 years and there was 14 of them.
